reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Leon sat on the big red couch at Mr. Kay's house. Everyone was watching the game on TV. The crowd on the screen was very loud.

"Who is winning?" Leon asked.

"The blue team," said Grandpa.

Ten minutes later, Leon asked again. "Who is winning now?"

Grandpa laughed. "My memory is like a frozen berry. It will not budge!"

Leon bit his snack and looked around the room. Then he saw it. A big sign on the TV, with numbers on it. The blue team had a big number. The red team had a small number.

Leon pointed at the sign. "Look! The blue team is winning!"

"That's the scoreboard," said Mr. Kay. "You found it all by yourself."

Now Leon did not need to ask. He just looked up at the numbers.

"Blue team is winning!" he shouted. "Blue team is winning again!"

Grandpa covered his ears and grinned. "Okay, okay. You are the score king now."

Leon took a string from his snack bag and held it up like a tiny flag. "Blue team! Blue team!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Daniel put his hands in the bowl. The dough was soft and very sticky. It stuck to his fingers like glue. "Oh no," said Daniel. "The bread is broken!"

His mom laughed a little. "Push it," she said. "Then fold it over." Daniel pushed the dough with his palm. He folded one side over the other. The dough felt smoother each time. He pushed and folded some more. Soon his fingers were clean. The dough was soft like a pillow.

Daniel made a round ball. "Look, Mom! I fixed it!" His mom put the ball on a safe tray. The teacher slid the tray into the big oven. Later the bread came out warm and puffy. Daniel held a piece for his dad. "I pushed it and folded it," he said. "Then it turned into bread!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Luca ran into the backyard. He wanted his blue ball. He had a big game to play!

But the ball was gone. Then he saw it. It had rolled under the old tent. The tent was very dark inside. Luca reached in with one hand. He felt something round. He pulled it out fast.

The thing was not blue. It was not a ball at all. It was a red bucket! Luca laughed. He reached in again. He felt a shovel. He felt a soft rag. He pulled the rag out and used it to clean the bucket. Then he felt one more round thing. He pulled it out into the sun. It was blue! It was his ball!

Luca jumped up and down. "The tent played hide and seek," he said. "And I won!" He threw the red bucket over his arm and ran to show Dad before bed. Dad clapped his hands. "Big news," said Dad. Luca was happy all the way to the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story: Wesley ran into the band room. He was going to play a violin today. His mom gave him a wave from the door. Wesley picked up the violin. He held it upside down. He tapped the strings. Plink, plonk. The sound was very silly. Wesley laughed. He tried again. Plink, plonk. Still silly. He swung the bow in the air like a stick. Still no pretty music. Wesley frowned. "Violin, you are mixed up," he said. Then Miss Poppy came over. "Let me show you how to hold it," she said. She turned the violin the right way up. She helped Wesley put it under his chin. Wesley pulled the bow. The violin sang. A long, sweet note filled the room. Wesley played it again and again. "Mom, listen!" he called. His mom clapped loud. After the lesson, she gave him a crunchy apple for the walk home. Wesley hummed his note all the way.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
John sat at the art table. He wanted to draw a sun. The sun needed a big circle in the middle. John drew and drew. But his circle came out wobbly and curly. It did not look like a sun. It looked like a wiggly worm.

John put down his crayon. Then he saw Maya next to him. Maya was tracing around her cup. She moved it slowly with one finger on top. When she lifted the cup, there was a perfect circle on her paper.

John picked up his own cup. He put it down on his paper. He traced all around the bottom. He lifted the cup away. There it was. A big round circle. John added curly rays and a happy face.

The teacher walked by with the hot glue gun. She held it up high. "This can burn," she said. "Only I touch it." John kept his fingers far away.

He held up his sun. "Look, Maya! A real circle!" Maya smiled and traced her cup again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Myles stood by the back door. He wanted to wear his sun hat and play outside. But the sky was full of clouds. "Where did the sun go?" he asked. "Maybe the clouds are hiding it," said Dad. Myles watched and waited. He saw a big gray cloud. It looked like a naughty turtle, slow and round.

Then the wind came. It was windy now! The leaves spun around. Myles felt the wind push his hair. "The wind is moving the clouds," he said. The big cloud slid away. The sun popped out! It was sunny again.

Myles put on his sun hat. He ran to the sandbox. The warm sun made the sand hot on top. "The sun makes things warm," said Myles. Then the sky turned dark again. Little drops fell. It was rainy now. Dad called, "Come get your rain boots!" Myles stomped in the puddles.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Camille wanted to see the bubbles. Mama was going to fill the pot with water. Camille stood by the door and watched.

"One step, two steps, three steps back," said Mama with a smile. Camille took three steps back. She was brave, but she stayed far away.

Mama put the pot on the stove. Soon the water went pop, pop, pop. Little clouds rose up from the pot. Camille saw the steam touch the window. The window got warm and foggy. Camille put her hand near her own cup of cold milk. Cold, not hot. Then she looked at the steam far away. Hot, hot, hot.

"Can I see the bubbles?" asked Camille.

"Come hold my hand," said Mama. Camille held Mama's hand. She peeked at the pot from far away. The bubbles went bloop, bloop, bloop.

"One cloud, two clouds, three clouds," said Camille, counting the steam. It floated up, up, up, like a dream.

"The steam is hot, so we stay back," said Camille.

Mama kissed her head. "Yes, my smart girl."

Camille watched the steam dance until it was time for warm oatmeal.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Madison found a box of old balls in the shed. "I will make a rainbow," she said. She picked up a red ball. She set it on the grass. Red went with red.

Next she found a blue ball. Blue went with blue. Then a yellow ball. Yellow went with yellow. Soon she had three piles, neat as can be. A green ball went in its own spot. "You are the grass color," she told it.

A little green snake slid by her shoe. Madison held very still. The snake was green too. "You can sit with the green ball," she whispered. The snake slid away into the bushes. A red ball was hiding in the blue pile. Madison laughed. She moved it to the red pile. Then she shut the shed door tight. "Night night, rainbow," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Sophie sat in the car. She sat in her deep car seat. Mom sat in front with a little bundle. The bundle was Sophie's new baby brother.

"I will hold him," said Mom. "He is so little." Mom looked at the baby all the way home. Sophie looked out the window.

At home, Dad said, "Cookie time." He gave Sophie a cookie. The baby slept. Mom fed the baby. Sophie ate her cookie alone.

"I miss you, Mom," said Sophie. "You held me before." Mom put the baby in his bed. Then Mom sat next to Sophie. "Come here," said Mom. Mom gave her a big hug.

Sophie hugged her back. Then the baby made a sound. Mom laughed. "He is calling you," she said. Sophie tiptoed to the bed. The baby grabbed her finger. "He likes me," said Sophie. Mom smiled and held them both.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Benjamin was playing house at daycare. He made a big pile of soft blocks. The blocks were his pretend mountain. His teddy bear was going to climb the mountain. "Climb, teddy, climb!" said Benjamin.

Then teddy fell off. He dropped right onto the floor. Mia saw it. Her lip began to shake. "Teddy fell!" she said. "He is hurt. He is scared."

Benjamin picked up teddy. He squeezed teddy tight. He patted teddy's soft head. "There, there," said Benjamin. "A hug helps."

Mia stopped crying. She wanted a turn too. She held teddy and rocked him. "Teddy feels better now," she said.

The teacher smiled. "Teddy can have a pretend snack too," she said. She handed them a tiny pretend cake.

"Teddy is hungry," said Mia. "Teddy will eat the cake!" said Benjamin.

Then teddy climbed the mountain again. This time he got all the way to the top.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Aurora ran into Grandma's house. Everyone was there! Aunt Mia was stirring a big pot. Grandma was setting out plates. The whole table smelled like bread and soup.

"Today you can lead the blessing," said Grandma. Aurora clapped her hands. She was so lucky! She had waited all year for this. But then Grandma began to sing. The blessing was a song, not just words.

Aurora opened her mouth. She tried the tune. It came out wrong! The notes went up when they should go down. Uncle Ben smiled at her. "Take your time," he said. "We can wait."

Aurora took a big breath. She thought of the song in her head. Then she tried again. This time the tune came out right! The whole family sang with her. Their voices filled the room. Baby cousin Sam kicked his feet to the song.

When the song ended, everyone said, "Amen!" Grandma kissed Aurora's head. "Now we eat!" said Aunt Mia. She carried the pot to the table, and Aurora passed out the spoons.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Violet held Mama's hand at the door of the big house. Inside, people were singing. Little lamps sat in rows along the front. Their small flames flickered like tiny stars.

"Can I light one?" Violet asked.

"Flames are for grown-ups," said Grandma. "But you can pick one for me to light."

Violet looked at all the lamps. Some were tall. Some were small. One had a red flower painted on the side. "That one," she said, pointing. "The flower one."

Grandma took a long match. She struck it carefully. A little flame jumped up on the match. Then Grandma touched it to the wick. The lamp with the flower lit up bright.

Violet watched with wide eyes. The match made the lamp glow. "It worked!" she said.

"You picked it, and I lit it," said Grandma. "We did it together."

Grandma blew out the match. The lamp kept shining. Its warm light made a soft circle on the wall. The flames were not scary at all. They were calm and small, and Grandma's hands held them safely.

Violet stood by her lamp while the people sang. She watched her flower flame dance. "Good night, little light," she whispered. "Stay warm until we come back."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Violet ran to school after breakfast. She was not late today. Outside, her friends were playing hide-and-seek.

"I will count," said Violet. "You go hide." She closed her eyes. "One, two, three!" Her friends ran. "Four, five, six!" They were still running. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Violet opened her eyes. Little Ben stood in the open. He had not found a spot.

"You counted too fast," Ben said. "We need time to hide."

"Okay," said Violet. "I will count slowly." She closed her eyes again. "One... two... three..." Her friends tiptoed away. "Four... five... six..." She heard soft steps behind the big tree. "Seven... eight... nine... ten!" Ready or not, here she came.

Ben was gone now. He was under the slide. Sam was behind the tree. Mia was by the wall. Violet found them all, one by one.

Then it was Ben's turn to count. Violet ran fast to hide. She heard him counting slowly, so she had time. She squeezed behind the bush just as he said, "Ten!"

"I found you, Violet!" Ben called. Violet laughed and popped out. "Count slowly again," she said. "That is the best way to play."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara loved her classroom. It had one big window and two small windows. At nap time, Miss Paz pulled the curtains shut. The room went dark. "Night, night," she said, and everyone slept.

Clara woke up. The room was dark. She thought it was night. "Night means home," she said. She looked for her coat. She walked slow, slow, slow, past the sleeping mats. A moth with one dusty wing sat on the wall. It looked just as mixed up as she felt.

Clara tugged Miss Paz's sleeve. "It is night," she said. "I want to go home." Miss Paz smiled. "Come and see," she said. She opened the curtains, one, two, three. The sun came in. The room turned bright and warm. The moth flew fast out the door. Outside, the day was wide and wild with light.

"Day," said Clara. "Not night. Day and night are not the same." She put her coat back. She lay down on her mat. She closed her eyes and waited, nice and slow, for snack time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
William loved his little red truck. He brought it to summer camp in his backpack.

At camp, a boy named Sam saw the truck. Sam reached out and grabbed it. "My turn!" said Sam. William grabbed it back. "No, it's mine!" Then the truck fell on the grass. Both boys looked at it.

Their teacher, Miss Ada, came over. She knelt down. "Sam, you can ask first," she said. Sam took a big breath. "Can I have a turn, please?" William held the truck tight. He did not want to let go. But he counted to ten, slow and quiet. Then he put the truck in Sam's hands.

Sam rolled the truck through the cool, green grass. He made a loud brmmmm sound. Then he gave it back. "Your turn," said Sam. William smiled. Taking turns felt good.

The next day, William's friend Ben came to play at camp. William left his red truck at home, tucked safe on his shelf. He brought a friendly blue ball instead. "Let's roll it!" said William. Ben rolled it first. William waited. Then it was his turn.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. She wore her red coat. The wind blew at the big doors. The wind made her coat fly open, flappy flappy, like bird wings.

"My coat is being silly," said Rehmat. Mama laughed. "You can fix it," she said. Rehmat looked down. She saw the little zipper tab. She pulled it up, up, up. The two sides of her coat came together. Click, click, click. Now the coat was closed. No more flapping.

Inside the bank, it was warm. Rehmat felt proud. She unzipped her coat a little bit, then zipped it again, just for fun. Zzzzzip. A man at the desk smiled at her. "You are a fast zipper," he said. Rehmat giggled.

After the bank, Mama bought Rehmat a shiny red apple. Rehmat held it in her zipped-up coat. "Sorry, apple, no room in there," she teased. She carried the apple in her hand instead. She skipped all the way home.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story: Luka was at summer camp. He sat at a big paint table. He had a pot of yellow. He had a pot of blue. He wanted to paint his mother a picture. He dipped his brush in the yellow. He made a big yellow sun. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue. He wanted a blue sky. But the sky came out green. Luka blinked at it. "Green?" he said. His friend Mia was shy. She peeked at his paper and smiled. Luka looked at his pots. The yellow pot was all green now. He tried to pull the green apart with his brush. He stirred and stirred. The green stayed green. "It will not come back," he said softly. The teacher gave him new pots. Luka was careful this time. He kept a little yellow in a cup. He kept a little blue in another cup. Then he mixed the rest. Green again! Luka laughed. He painted his mother a sun, a sky, and a green grass snake. "Look, Mom," he said. "I made a new color!"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Joshua ran into the cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family. "One, two, three, four cups of flour," he counted.

First came the stirring. Joshua loved to stir. Round and round went the spoon. The batter looked like soft mud. It smelled sweet like cake.

Now he needed butter. Joshua got some from the fridge. He tried to spread it on his bread. The butter was hard. It tore a big hole. "Naughty butter!" said Joshua.

Miss Amy put the butter on the counter. "We will wait," she said. Joshua waited. He counted to ten. Then he touched the butter. It was soft now. It spread like a dream.

Joshua carried the warm bread home. "I made this!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. There was a big red truck on the rug. Charlie wanted the truck. But Ben had the truck first.

Charlie reached out fast. Her hand almost grabbed it. Her teacher, Miss Ana, sat down next to her. "You can have a turn next," Miss Ana said. She set a little timer on the table. Charlie watched the timer. Tick, tick, tick.

Then the timer rang. Ben held the truck up high. He looked like he might toss it. Charlie held her hands out, soft and open. Ben put the truck in her hands, gently, one wheel at a time. Charlie smiled. The truck had a scratch on its side. She turned it over. The wheels felt bumpy. She rolled it across the rug. It bumped over her leg and kept going.

Soon the timer rang again. Charlie stood up. She walked to a girl named Mia. "Here," Charlie said. She handed the truck over, gently, just like Ben had done. Mia hugged the truck. Then something surprising happened. Mia rolled it back to Charlie, so they could both play.

Miss Ana clapped her hands. Charlie sat close to Mia. They rolled the truck back and forth. Then they all had cake.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Miles sat in the family car. He held his blanket tight. “First haircut today,” said Mom. The car stopped at the salon.

Inside, a chair went up and down. Miles climbed in. The hairdresser sprayed his hair. It felt wet and cool. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little curls dropped onto the cape. One curl landed on Miles’s hand. He picked it up. Mom held out a small envelope. She tucked the curl inside. “A little hair from your first haircut,” she said. “To keep.”

Miles watched the envelope close. “That curl is mine?” he asked. “Yes,” said Mom. “Now we can look at it any time.” Miles put the envelope in his pocket. He marched back to the car with his blanket. In his pocket, the little curl rode home.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Parker made a painting at school. He wanted to give it to his mom as a gift. But the paint was wet. "The paint is not dry yet," said Miss Ana. "You can take it home later." Parker put it on the shelf to wait.

After lunch, Parker had nap time. He slept a long time. When he woke up, he said, "Is it morning now?" Miss Ana smiled. "No, Parker. It is afternoon now. A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night." Parker looked out the window. The sun was lower in the sky.

"Where is my painting?" he asked. "It is right here," said Miss Ana. It was not missing after all. The paint was dry now. Parker carried his gift to his cubby. "I will give it to Mom today," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Anna looked in the sandbox. No bunny. She looked behind the slide. No bunny. Her soft bunny was lost on the school playground.

Anna looked by the swings. No bunny. She sat down on the short wall. "Bunny is lost," she said. Her big sister Lily came over. "I will help you look," said Lily.

Anna and Lily looked by the park gate. No bunny. Then Dad came to pick Anna up. "I will help too," said Dad. Now three people were looking. Anna looked under the bench. Lily looked by the big tree. Dad looked in the little playhouse. Then Anna heard Dad call, "Come here!" There was bunny, sitting on the shelf. Anna hugged her bunny tight. "More looking eyes found you," said Anna. Lily smiled and helped Anna fold bunny's ears down soft.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Milo went to the park with his dad. There was a big hoop on the grass. There were beanbags in a basket. Milo wanted to throw one in.

He threw the beanbag up high. He thought it would bounce. He thought it would bounce right into the hoop. But it did not bounce. It went flop, down on the grass.

Milo picked it up. He threw it again. Flop. Then he stood close to the hoop. He threw it soft and straight. The beanbag went in. It landed with a little flop right inside.

Then Dad brought a big ball. "Catch with both hands," said Dad. Milo held out both hands. The ball was too fast. It bumped his tummy. He sat down and felt dizzy for a second. Dad sat down too. "Try again," said Dad.

Milo stood up. He held out both arms. Dad rolled the ball slow. Milo caught it with both hands. He hugged the ball tight.

"You did it," said Dad. Milo laughed and threw the ball back.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eli sits at the little table at daycare. He wants to write a note for Grandpa. Grandpa picks him up after snack. Eli holds his crayon. He writes letters all across the top of the paper. The letters run on and on, like one long worm.

Miss Amy sits next to him. "Can you read it to me?" she asks. Eli looks at his paper. He tries to read it. "Ilovyougranpa," he says fast, all in one breath. He frowns. "Grandpa can't find the words," Eli says.

"Where does one word stop?" Miss Amy asks. Eli points. "I. Love. You." He makes a space with his finger after each word. He writes the note again. This time he leaves a space between the words.

At pickup, Grandpa reads the note out loud. "I love you, Grandpa." He gives Eli a big hug. "You wrote this all by yourself." Eli smiles and holds the paper up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Lena stood on her stool in the kitchen. Today was Dad's birthday. Lena was going to make the cake!

She cracked the eggs. She poured the flour. She stirred and stirred. The batter was runny and wet.

"Yuck!" said Lena. "This is not a cake. It is soup!"

She thought about Dad's fox cup. It had a fox on it. Dad would want a real cake, not soup.

"Will it ever be a cake?" Lena asked Mom.

"Watch and see," said Mom.

Mom slid the pan into the oven. Lena sat on the floor and watched. She could not see inside.

Then the kitchen began to smell warm and sweet. Lena sniffed and sniffed.

The timer rang. Mom put on her big mitts. She pulled out the pan.

It was a cake! A real cake! Lena could poke it. It was soft, not runny.

"It worked!" Lena yelled. "The soup turned into cake!"

That night, Dad cut a slice. Lena took a big bite.

"Best cake ever," said Dad. "Happy birthday to me!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lillian went to the cultural center with Mama and Baba. It was Lunar New Year. There were red lanterns everywhere. Lillian held Mama's hand.

Then the drums began. Boom, boom, boom! They were so noisy. Lillian jumped and covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. Mama held her hand tight. Baba pointed at the door.

A big lion came in! It was red and gold. Its big mouth opened and closed. The lion moved to the drum beat. Lillian peeked at the lion. Boom, boom! The lion stomped. Boom, boom! The lion jumped high.

Lillian let go of her ears. She looked at the lion. She clapped one time. Then she clapped again. The lion shook its head at her. Lillian laughed. Baba clapped too. Mama clapped too. Lillian clapped with the noisy drums, boom, boom, boom.

The lion came close. It blinked its big eyes at Lillian. Lillian patted its soft nose. "More drums," she said. The drums went boom, boom, boom.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Henry put on his red shoe. Then he put on the other one. "Are we going on the big trip now?" he asked. "Yes!" said Dad. "We are going to the airport!"

Henry sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. The sky looked dark and stormy. "Will the rain stop us?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "Planes can fly after rain."

Soon they got to the airport. Henry saw the big planes. They were huge! He wanted to run to them. He took one step. Then he saw all the people. So many legs, so many bags!

Henry stopped. He ran back and grabbed Dad's hand. "Hold hands," he said. Dad smiled and held on tight. They walked close together, all the way.

At the window, Henry saw a plane go up into the sky. "Look, Dad! It's flying!" said Henry. Dad lifted him up high. "Our plane is next," said Dad. Henry squeezed his hand even tighter.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Ibrahim looked out the big window. He saw white snow falling down. "Snowy day!" he said. He put on his boots and his coat. He ran outside with Dad.

Ibrahim made a snowball with his bare hands. Brrr! His hands felt cold. They were very, very cold. He ran back to Dad. Dad helped him put on his red mittens. Then his hands felt warm again. "Good mittens," said Ibrahim. He made a new snowball. This one was big and round.

Then Ibrahim heard a funny beep, beep, beep. It came from the porch. It was his toy robot! Mom had set it outside in the snow. The robot beeped and its lights blinked. "My robot sees the snow," said Ibrahim. He remembered to bring it inside. He held it in his warm, mitten hands all the way to the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Evelyn sat on the red rug. Mama put on a song. The song went clippety, clippety, clippety.

Evelyn wanted to clap along. She clapped fast. Then the song got mixed up. Mama smiled. "Try clapping when I clap," she said.

Mama clapped one, two, one, two. Evelyn watched her hands. Evelyn clapped one, two, one, two. The claps fit the song. Evelyn laughed and clapped some more.

Then Mama sang a rhyme. "The cat sat on the mat. The cat put on a..." Mama stopped. "What comes next?"

Evelyn thought hard. She looked at her toy box. A hat sat on top of the blocks. "Hat!" said Evelyn. "The cat put on the hat!"

"Hat sounds like mat," said Mama. "You found it." Evelyn put the hat on her own head. Then she sang the whole rhyme, all by herself.

"Again!" said Evelyn, and she clapped one, two, one, two.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Kinsley went to the park with her dad. She wanted to play with the red ball. But the red ball rolled away from her. It rolled under the slide. The slide was wet and slippery. Kinsley could not reach the ball.

"Please help me, Dad," she said. Dad reached under the slide. He got the red ball out. He gave it to Kinsley. "Thank you," said Kinsley. Dad smiled.

Then a boy named Ben came over. Kinsley passed the ball to him. Ben ran off with the ball. He ran all the way to the sandbox. Then Ben stopped. He turned around. He came back and said, "Thank you!" Kinsley laughed. She passed the ball again. Now they took turns. Dad sat on the square bench and watched. The sun came out. The slide was dry. "My turn," said Kinsley, and up she went.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Paisley held Mama's hand at the shelter. Cats and dogs sat in little rooms. They were all waiting for a family. Paisley walked past a big dog. She walked past a fluffy cat. Then she saw a small gray kitten. The kitten put one paw out. "Hello," said Paisley.

The kitten came home with them. Paisley wanted to feed her right away. But the kitten hid under the sofa. "She is scared," said Mama. "Let's make her a soft spot." Paisley put a little blanket by the sofa. Then she put down a small bowl of food. Paisley waited very still.

The moon came up in the window. The kitten peeked out. She sniffed the blanket. She sniffed the bowl. Then she climbed onto the blanket and ate. Paisley saw it all. Her soft spot made the kitten come out.

Paisley sat by the blanket with her own yummy snack. The kitten finished eating. She walked to Paisley and rubbed her small head on Paisley's knee. "Good night, kitten," Paisley whispered. The kitten curled up on the blanket and closed her eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Georgia put on her big farm hat. The hat was loose and wobbled on her head. "I want to help today," she said.

Farmer Ada smiled. "Can you sort these for me?" She put a feather, a pinecone and a small blanket on the grass. "Put the soft ones here. Put the rough ones there."

Georgia picked up the pinecone. It poked her fingers. She set it down fast. Then she touched the feather. It was light and soft like a kiss. "Soft!" she said. She put it in the soft pile. She touched the blanket. It was warm and soft too. "Soft," she said again.

The pinecone waited in the grass. Georgia touched it one more time. Her fingers said poke, poke. "Rough," she said. She put it in the rough pile all by herself.

Farmer Ada clapped. "Your hands can tell you that," she said. Georgia patted her own fingers. Then she sniffed the feather. She smelled hay and sunshine. "My nose knows things too," she said. She hugged the soft blanket tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Olivia got to school with her coat on. Teacher Sam pointed at the big clock. "Time to play inside!" Inside, Olivia ran and jumped. She got warm.

Olivia wanted her coat off. She pulled the little zipper tab. She pulled it down, down, down. The coat opened all by itself! Olivia slid her arms out. Then she was not too warm anymore.

Later it was time to go outside. Olivia put her arms back in the sleeves. She pulled the tab up, up, up. The coat closed. She did it all by herself.

Teacher Sam smiled. "Nice work, Olivia. You did that all alone."

Olivia looked at her friend Ben. His coat had a different zipper. His was red. Hers was blue.

"My turn again tomorrow," said Olivia. She zipped it up one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Axel sat at the dinner table. He wiggled a tooth. It felt loose. "It is almost missing!" he said. Mom smiled. Dad put carrots on Axel's plate.

"How many days until Saturday?" Axel asked. Saturday was pancake day. He could not wait. "Count with me," said Dad. Axel held up his hands. He touched each finger, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers stood up tall.

"Seven days make a week," said Dad. Axel frowned. He counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Still seven. He touched his thumb last. The loose tooth wiggled again. "So Saturday comes after all seven days?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. Axel jumped in his seat.

Then Axel began to sing. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" He sang it twice. He ate his carrots fast. "I will not forget," he said. "Seven days. Then pancakes." He touched his thumb one more time and grinned. The tooth wobbled like a tiny door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Milan ran to school with a big question. "Is today the library day?" he asked his teacher. She smiled and said, "Yes, today is the day. Today is happening right now." Milan jumped up and down. Yesterday he had waited and waited. Tomorrow would be too late. Today was here.

The class walked to the library. Milan held his coin tight in his pocket. He wanted to cook up a plan for story time later. First, the teacher read a bright book about trains. Then the librarian said, "Now you may pick your own book." Milan looked and looked. The shelves were tall. He pulled one book out. Too big. He tried again and again. His friend waited with him, patient and quiet.

At last Milan found a small red book. He gave his coin to the librarian for the late fee, just like Mom had shown him. "Now we read," said the teacher. Milan sat down on the soft rug. He opened his book, and the first page showed a bright yellow truck. "Later I will read it to my mom," Milan said. "But now I read it here."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson ran to the table. Lunch was there. He could smell the warm noodles. But his hands were muddy from the yard. He touched the table, and one brown mark showed up. His mama saw the mark. "Hands first," she said. She pointed to the sink.

Jaxson went to the sink. Mama turned on the water. It felt cool and soft. He rubbed his hands. One, two, three rubs. The mud went down, down, down. Now his hands were clean and pink. He dried them on the small towel. It was soft like a cloud.

Jaxson came back to the table. He held up his hands. No mud now. He ate his noodles. They were warm and yummy. Then he saw something. His fork had a noodle hanging off it. It swung like a little rope. Jaxson laughed.

After lunch, Jaxson helped pick up his plate. The water in his cup made a tiny wave. His baby sister, a little girl with one tooth, clapped her hands. "Ba!" she said. Jaxson clapped too. Then he asked for more noodles. "More, please," he said. Mama smiled and filled his bowl again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zoe packed her little red bag. "We go to the big park today!" she said. Daddy opened the car door for her. Zoe climbed into her seat. Mama buckled her in. The wheels went round and round on the road.

At the park, Zoe saw tall trees. She saw a big lake. A deer walked near the water. Zoe waved at the deer. It looked at her and walked away. "Bye bye, deer," said Zoe.

Mama held up her phone. "Smile, Zoe," said Mama. Click! The phone took a photo. Zoe saw her own face on the little screen. "That is me!" she said. Zoe pointed at a big rock. "Photo the rock too, Mama!" Click!

The sun went down. Zoe was very tired. Daddy carried her to the car. "I miss the deer," said Zoe. Mama opened the photos. "Look, here is the deer," she said. Zoe touched the screen. "Deer!" she said, and smiled. In the morning, Zoe looked at the photos again. "More park photos, Mama," she said. "Yes," said Mama. "All day long."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Billie helped Mom in the kitchen. Mom turned on the stove. "Is it hot?" Billie asked. "Yes, very hot," said Mom. Billie stood back and watched. Mom cracked eggs into a bright yellow bowl. "We need more eggs," said Mom. "Let's go to the store."

At the store, Billie's arms wanted to swing. She swung them as she walked. Then she looked up. Mom was not there. Billie did not see her coat. She did not see her shoes.

Billie saw a lady at the checkout. The lady had a bright vest on. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. The lady smiled and picked up her phone. Soon Mom came around the corner. "Billie! There you are," said Mom. She gave Billie a big hug. "Can I help with the eggs now?" Billie asked. "You can hold the carton," said Mom. Billie held it all the way to the car.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Hayden wants to brush his teeth like a big lion. He holds his little toothbrush with both hands. The sink is cold when he touches it. Brrr! Then Mama turns the tap for him. She puts her hand under first. "Too hot," she says. She waits. She turns the tap a little. The water gets warm.

Hayden brushes his teeth. He roars like a lion at the mirror. Then he sees something on the shelf. Small red dots in a bottle. They look like candy. Hayden reaches up. "Wait," says Mama. She takes the bottle down. "These are not candy. They are special medicine. Only a grown-up gives it to you." Hayden puts his hands behind his back. He looks and looks at the red dots. He does not touch them.

Mama puts the bottle high up on a shelf. Hayden points at it. "Medicine," he says. "Only a big person." Mama smiles. She hands him his special lion cup. Hayden drinks his cool water. "Roar," he says.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Aaron brought his red car to school. At play time, he rode the big tricycle around the playground. Then he played in the sandbox. Then he went on the slide. "Where is my car?" Aaron said. His pockets were empty.

His teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Where did you go first?" she asked. "The tricycle," said Aaron. He walked back to the tricycles. He looked under the wheels. No car. Next he had played in the sand. He walked to the sandbox. He dug gently with his hands. Still no car.

The sky was cloudy, but the sand was dry. "One more place," said Aaron. He walked to the slide. He looked at the bottom. There, in the grass, sat his red car! "I went back to every place, in the same order," Aaron said. Miss Kim clapped. "You found it, Aaron!" Aaron held his car up high and ran to show his friend Ben.
